title: ‘I know that treasure does not last’
theme: Death says he knows that what is called treasure does not last and that the lasting is not reached by things that pass; yet he built the Nāciketa fire of perishable things and obtained ‘the lasting’ — a puzzle each commentator resolves in his own way.

words.role: main verb of the first sentence

words.context: Śaṅkara: «पुनरपि तुष्ट आह» — Death, pleased again, speaks

words.role: subject of the clause closed by iti
words.context: Śaṅkara: «निधिः कर्मफललक्षणः», the treasure that is the fruit of action
Madhva: «अध्रुवैस्तद्भक्तिवर्जितैर्न प्राप्यते», means without devotion to the Lord

words.gram: past active participle m. nom. sg.

words.context: Śaṅkara: «नित्यमापेक्षिकं», permanent only by comparison; Madhva: «नित्यं भगवन्तं»

sandhi.rule: i before a vowel becomes y, P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि).
The final s of śevadhiḥ (P. 8.2.66 (ससजुषो रुँः)) is r before a vowel after i; iti + anityam give ity anityam, P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि).
hi + adhruvaiḥ give hy adhruvaiḥ, P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि).
The visarga after a becomes u before a voiced consonant, P. 6.1.114 (हशि च), and a + u give o, P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः).

sandhi.type: visarga before c; aḥ before a; visarga as r
sandhi.rule: nāciketaḥ before c becomes nāciketaś, P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः) with P. 8.4.40 (स्तोः श्चुना श्चुः). citaḥ before a becomes cito and the a is elided (avagraha), P. 6.1.113 (अतो रोरप्लुतादप्लुते), P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः), P. 6.1.109 (एङः पदान्तादति). agniḥ and anityaiḥ keep r before a vowel and before d.

samasa.meaning: impermanent (also anityaiḥ in the second line)

morphology.note: A neuter predicate with the masculine śevadhiḥ: ‘[is] an impermanent thing’. Śaṅkara restates it in the masculine: «असौ अनित्यम् अनित्य इति जानामि».
Taddhita (vṛddhi of the first syllable) from Naciketas: the fire named after the boy in 1.1.16 (‘by your name shall this fire be known’). Madhva’s text reads the vocative naciketaḥ (see ambiguities).
Past passive participle of √ci ‘pile, build up’: the fire altar is piled of bricks.
Past active participle in -vat of pra-√āp; with asmi it gives a past sense, ‘I have obtained’.

translation.literal: I know [that what is called] treasure [is] impermanent; for that permanent [one] is not obtained by unstable [things]. Therefore by me the Nāciketa fire was built with impermanent materials; [by it] I have obtained the permanent.
translation.readable: I know that what people call treasure does not last, and that what is lasting is not reached through things that pass. That is why I built the Nāciketa fire out of perishable things — and through it I have reached what lasts.

anvaya: अहम् शेवधिः इति [यत् उच्यते तत्] अनित्यम् [इति] जानामि । हि अध्रुवैः तत् ध्रुवम् न हि प्राप्यते । ततः मया अनित्यैः द्रव्यैः नाचिकेतः अग्निः चितः, [तेन] नित्यम् प्राप्तवान् अस्मि ।
syntax: The first line holds a statement of knowledge (jānāmy ahaṃ … iti) and its reason (na hy … tat). The second draws a consequence (tataḥ) in two clauses: a passive one (mayā … citaḥ agniḥ, ‘the fire was built by me’) and an active periphrasis (prāptavān asmi, ‘I have obtained’). The speaker is not named in the verse.

ambiguities.note: The first line says the permanent is not reached by impermanent means; the second says that Death, building a fire of impermanent things, obtained the permanent. Śaṅkara: the ‘permanent’ is relative, Death’s own station, which lasts long compared with human pleasures — «नित्यं याम्यं स्थानं स्वर्गाख्यं नित्यमापेक्षिकं प्राप्तवानस्मि». Raṅgarāmānuja: the fire was built for the sake of the knowledge that leads to Brahman, so what was obtained is that knowledge, the means to the eternal fruit — «नित्यफलसाधनं ज्ञानं प्राप्तवानस्मि इत्यर्थः». Madhva: the permanent is the Lord, and the ‘materials’ are the mind and the like directed to him — «नित्यं भगवन्तं प्राप्तवानस्मि».

Śaṅkara and Raṅgarāmānuja introduce the verse as Death speaking again, pleased (Śaṅkara: «पुनरपि तुष्ट आह»). Madhva’s text reads naciketaḥ, a vocative, for nāciketaḥ: ‘therefore, Naciketas, the fire was built by me …’ (corrections.json).

metre.name: triṣṭubh
metre.note: Triṣṭubh, 22 + 23 syllables: pādas of 11, 11, 11 and 12. The last pāda (anityair dravyaiḥ prāptavān asmi nityam) has twelve syllables in every witness; Madhva’s compound anityadravyaiḥ does not change the count.

beginner: Death speaks again, pleased with the boy, and admits something about himself. He knows that what people call treasure — the rewards that rituals and good works bring — does not last. He knows too that something lasting cannot be bought with things that pass. Yet he once built the fire altar named after Naciketas out of perishable things, and he says that through it he reached what lasts. How can both be true? The commentators answer differently. Śaṅkara says Death’s position lasts only by comparison with ours: it is long, not eternal. Raṅgarāmānuja says Death built the fire for the sake of knowledge, and it is knowledge, not the bricks, that leads to the eternal. Madhva says what was reached is the Lord, approached with a mind turned toward him. All three keep the first line: the permanent cannot be purchased.
analogy: Like paying for a ladder with coins: the ladder can lift you to a high shelf, but no number of coins becomes the sky.

commentary.q: What does Death say he knows?
commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: That treasure is impermanent, that the permanent is not reached by unstable things, and that he nevertheless built the Nāciketa fire with impermanent materials and obtained ‘the permanent’.

commentary.q: How can the impermanent obtain the permanent?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: the treasure is the fruit of action, «निधिः कर्मफललक्षणः». The truly permanent treasure, the supreme Self, is not obtained by impermanent means — «तत् प्राप्यते परमात्माख्यः शेवधिः» is denied of them. What Death won by the fire is his own post, heaven, permanent only by comparison: «तेनाहमधिकारापन्नो नित्यं याम्यं स्थानं स्वर्गाख्यं नित्यमापेक्षिकं प्राप्तवानस्मि».

commentary.q: What did the fire win, on Raṅgarāmānuja’s reading?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The fire was built with bricks and the like for the sake of the knowledge that is the means to Brahman — «ब्रह्मप्राप्तिसाधनज्ञानोद्देशेन अनित्यैः इष्टकादिद्रव्यैः नाचिकेतोऽग्निश्चितः» — and so what Death obtained is knowledge, the means to the eternal fruit: «नित्यफलसाधनं ज्ञानं प्राप्तवानस्मि इत्यर्थः». Brahman remains reached by knowledge alone.

commentary.q: Madhva: the permanent is the Lord
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Madhva reads nityam as the Lord: «नित्यं भगवन्तं प्राप्तवानस्मि । ध्रुवो भगवान्». The unstable means are those without devotion to him — «अध्रुवैस्तद्भक्तिवर्जितैर्न प्राप्यते» — and the materials are the mind and the like: «द्रव्यैर्मन आदिभिः».

commentary.q: Madhva’s text and the vishvAsa mūla
commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: Madhva’s mūla reads naciketaḥ (vocative) for nāciketaḥ, and the compound anityadravyaiḥ for anityair dravyaiḥ. The vishvAsa mūla writes agniḥ anityaiḥ with the visarga kept, an orthographic difference (corrections.json).

advaita.text: The fire wins only a relative permanence, Death’s own station — «नित्यमापेक्षिकं». The eternal treasure, the supreme Self, is not reached by such means.

visistadvaita.text: The fire was built for the sake of knowledge, and knowledge is what was gained: «नित्यफलसाधनं ज्ञानं प्राप्तवानस्मि इत्यर्थः». Brahman is still reached by knowledge alone.

dvaita.text: The permanent obtained is the Lord — «ध्रुवो भगवान्» — who is not reached by means without devotion.

schools.disagreement: All three keep the first line’s principle. They differ on what ‘the permanent’ of the second line is: Death’s relatively lasting station (Śaṅkara), the knowledge that leads to Brahman (Raṅgarāmānuja), or the Lord (Madhva).

parallels.note: The Muṇḍaka: the unmade is not won by what is made — the principle of the first line.

contemporary.text: Some goals are reached by effort and money, and some are not. Death’s admission — I know treasure does not last — is followed by an honest account of what his own effort bought. A modern reader might take from it the habit of asking, of any large investment of time or money, what kind of thing it can buy and what kind it cannot. This is a reflection, not a claim made by the text.

reflect.beginner: What have you worked hard for that turned out to last less long than you expected?
reflect.deeper: Can something lasting be reached by means that do not last? Which of the three readings of the second line seems most honest to you, and why?
reflect.practice: Before your next large purchase or commitment, write down what you hope it will give you, and whether it is the kind of thing that can give it.

flags.note: Madhva’s text reads naciketaḥ (vocative) for nāciketaḥ and anityadravyaiḥ for anityair dravyaiḥ (corrections.json).
What ‘the permanent’ (nityam) of the second line is: Death’s station (Śaṅkara), knowledge (Raṅgarāmānuja), the Lord (Madhva).
